Of bots, watts, and waterpremium

Hosting foreign dignitaries outside Delhi not a new practice, says MEA

 Unlike their devoted base, Mr Modi and Mr Shah are realistic about Rahul because they know their politics. Rahul’s followers and Mr Modi agree on one thing, and they’re both right that however consistently Rahul may have faltered in the past, the Congress under him poses the only credible challenge to the BJP. See it this way. From its lowest Lok Sabha tally of 44 seats in 2014 through 52 in 2019 to 99 in 2024, the Congress vote share has been steady in the 19-21 per cent range. That’s one in five Indians instinctively voting for the “hand” symbol. Looking at data from 1996 through 2009, the BJP floated within the 25 per cent ballpark. That’s one in four voters. It was the coalition era. Mr Modi changed that equation in 2014. The BJP has floated in the 37-40 per cent range since. A jump of 12-15 percentage points over the baseline is phenomenal and devastating in a multi-party system. We can safely call this top-up the Modi vote. It’s unrealistic to imagine Rahul taking the Congress vote share to 37 per cent in the foreseeable future. But, if he simply adds another 5-6 per cent to his core vote, national politics changes. He’s been routinely losing 9 out of 10 direct fights against the BJP. You can then presume that most of this vote will come from the BJP in regions it routinely sweeps. The 2024 election was a limited coalition exception. As the Opposition vote consolidated, BJP’s strike rate declined. It won only 7 out of every 10 direct contests against the Congress. A BJP at 32 per cent will still dominate, but its Lok Sabha numbers could fall to low-200s or even below that. It may still form a government, but it will be a genuine National Democratic Alliance coalition, with all the attendant leadership complications. That’s the threat Mr Modi and Mr Shah have never taken lightly. They don’t believe Rahul is their best asset in the Opposition. They know that the Congress, with its one-in-five vote base, is their only challenger. And the Congress, like it or not, can’t stay intact without the Gandhis. Now, the key point: Where does this take Rahul? At this time, he’s totally focused on building the “street” against Mr Modi. He’s willing to partner anybody, from mostly apolitical CJP to hard-Left All India Students’ Association, from Abhijeet Dipke to Neha Bora. Having been through the school of hard knocks since he joined politics in 2004, Rahul should know that political change in India is brought about either by those who win an election, or combine with others to defeat an incumbent. A “regime change” on the streets is an empty hard-Left fantasy because they can never win an election. The combined might of Jayaprakash Narayan (Navnirman Andolan) and George Fernandes (Railway Strike), backed by the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and Lohiaite street power and armed with that Allahabad High Court order, couldn’t topple Indira Gandhi. They had to wait for the 1977 election. In 2010-12, a dead-in-the-water United Progressive Alliance wasn’t thrown out by the Anna movement and RSS/BJP. It took the 2014 election to settle the issue. The next general election in 2029 will mark 25 years in politics for Rahul. He will still be only 59, young by the standards of Indian politics. But presuming that the Congress and the BJP retain their ideologically frozen vote, Mr Modi’s add-on voters won’t shift to Rahul out of boredom. He has to offer them a better, constructive, optimistic proposition. What will he do differently from Modi/BJP if elected? Let me list just a dozen short questions: 
  • How would he want Election Commissioners to be picked and the impartiality of Election Commission of India restored? Return to the Congress/UPA era isn’t inspiring. His late father had tried in 1989 to weaken the EC by making it a three-member body. Further, how will he ensure that non-citizens (those the BJP has labelled ghuspethiyas) don’t become voters?
  • The same for the judiciary, CBI and the other key agencies.
  • How will he handle a Trump-like challenge? How will his policy towards the United States be any different?
  • What’s his plan to deal with the Chinese? How will his treatment of Pakistan and terrorism emanating from there be different? Softer than Modi’s, or harder?
  • How will his approach to West Asia and Israel differ from Modi’s?
  • What’s his vision for managing India’s chronic and crippling triple-shortage of energy, capital and gold? We can add AI/software services to this now. How will he make India a magnet for investors?
  • Chhatron ki Goonj is resonating. But how will he create more jobs? Further, for the less educated, will he restore MGNREGA, or introduce a “new, improved” version? Will he continue giving away free food grains?
  • Is caste Census still his idea of social justice? How will it create more jobs? Revanth Reddy doesn’t know what to do with his caste Census. Will he ask D K Shivakumar to at least release his caste Census data?
  • What changes does he plan for the education system to end corruption and profiteering, improve the quality of education, and make the young more employable?
  • He says he isn’t anti-business or anti-capital. He just wants no monopoly and a level playing field. How will he ensure that? What’s his concept of economic reform?
  • Since he and his “secular” partners complain that the minorities are marginalised, how would he mainstream them?
  • And finally, who is, or will be on his team?
 To look like a credible challenger and not just a street-fighter, Rahul needs to answer these questions and offer voters in the “middle” new ideas. Mr Modi started promising “Achche Din” by late 2012. At about the same distance from 2029, what’s Rahul promising? If he were to think out of the box, he could set up a UK-style shadow Cabinet. His “ministers” could then start answering these questions in their respective domains. Of course, if I were to be only part facetious, it could unleash mighty infighting even for these non-jobs. Whatever Rahul Gandhi chooses, he can’t go into 2029 again riding on his ecosystem’s clamour over Modi’s “falling” popularity. That has failed thrice already.

Deng Xiaoping’s reforms combined investment in education and research with technology transfers, overseas study and collaboration between foreign experts and Chinese institutions. India, by contrast, often fails to provide returning professionals with adequate research facilities or a welcoming institutional environment. Saran argues that promoting skilled migration while struggling to create meaningful domestic employment reflects a policy failure. With artificial intelligence becoming strategically crucial, he urges India to expand its existing centres of excellence and attract overseas talent to strengthen its scientific and technological capabilities.  Family-owned businesses face a persistent tension between cultural preferences for family leadership and the need to appoint the most competent executives. Succession requires clear distinctions between ownership, governance and management, alongside rigorous assessment and mentoring of potential heirs. R Gopalakrishnan recommends succession committees comprising family members and independent directors, with successors tested through challenging assignments and professional chief executives appropriately recognised. Brazil’s JBS offers an example: after its founder’s sons presided over rapid expansion and a corruption scandal, professional CEO Gilberto Tomazoni led the company for eight years before handing over to the founder’s grandson, who had undergone extensive grooming. Rahul Gandhi’s political prospects present a paradox: while BJP supporters dismiss him, Narendra Modi and Amit Shah treat the Congress leader as a serious challenger. The Congress retains a substantial vote base, and Shekhar Gupta argues that even a modest increase could significantly alter parliamentary arithmetic. But street mobilisation and allegations of electoral manipulation cannot substitute for a constructive alternative. With 2029 approaching, Gupta challenges Rahul to spell out policies on institutions, foreign affairs, jobs, caste, education, economic reform and minority inclusion. He might consider adopting a UK-style shadow cabinet to develop credible alternatives, given that criticism of Modi alone will not suffice. Growing resistance to data centres reflects their heavy consumption of power and water, limited job creation and concerns over privacy and political favouritism. Ukrainian drone attacks on Yandex facilities in Russia also highlight their vulnerability and potential role in hosting malicious online activity. In the US, opposition has become bipartisan, with some states considering moratoriums, while European projects face delays. Devangshu Datta cautions that India, despite the opportunity to attract investments displaced from Western markets, faces tighter resource constraints. Local resistance could grow if communities see few benefits, and might even limit losses if the AI investment boom collapses.

Today's editorials and columns examine the IDBI Bank privatisation deal, India's steel ambitions, tribunal reforms, AI-driven infrastructure improvements and a book on the changing geopolitical order

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 16 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page. The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs has approved the strategic sale of IDBI Bank, with Toronto-based Fairfax Financial Holdings set to acquire a 60.72 per cent stake for ₹52,878 crore. The deal, the largest foreign direct investment in India’s financial sector to date, offers an opportunity to revive the government’s stalled privatisation programme. Only 21 strategic sales have occurred in 26 years, while the number of central public-sector enterprises has risen. Today's first editorial argues that privatisation would free public resources and reduce fiscal burdens. It urges the government to sell its residual IDBI stake and accelerate equity sales in other public-sector companies. The draft National Steel Policy: Vision 2047 targets crude steel capacity of 604 million tonnes by 2047, but today's second editorial cautions that expansion must be matched by raw-material security, cleaner technology and global competitiveness. With India importing 92 per cent of its coking coal, greater reliance on conventional steelmaking could deepen import dependence and emissions. The policy’s proposals on scrap, renewable energy and hydrogen-based production need commercially viable implementation. Protection against unfair imports must not weaken incentives to improve productivity, particularly as carbon-related trade barriers spread. Our editorial also questions production-linked incentives, stressing that success depends on efficiency, innovation and higher-value products. India’s tribunals suffer from inadequate infrastructure, vacancies and administrative shortcomings, undermining their ability to deliver timely, specialised justice. K P Krishnan argues that the proposed National Tribunals Commission (NTC) must address these systemic failures rather than function merely as a personnel and oversight body. Drawing on the UK’s Courts and Tribunals Service and India’s Passport Seva model, he advocates separating judicial decision-making from administrative support. A professionally managed institution should handle procurement, infrastructure, technology and staffing, allowing judges to focus on adjudication. The NTC legislation offers an opportunity to build this institutional capacity and strengthen state capability across the economy. India’s artificial intelligence (AI) dividend could lie as much in improving existing infrastructure as in building new technology. Vinayak Chatterjee explores how machine learning, predictive maintenance and computer vision can help power networks, water systems, roads and railways detect faults early, reduce losses and improve reliability. India’s smart-meter rollout and Jal Jeevan Mission offer opportunities to apply these tools at scale, while examples from Sweden, Britain and Italy demonstrate their potential. However, fragmented records, incompatible systems and cybersecurity risks remain obstacles. Chatterjee advocates starting with targeted pilots, measuring operational gains and retaining human oversight, arguing that reliable data and effective implementation matter more than technological novelty. In The World in Turmoil: Why Geopolitics Matters, John Andrews examines how geography, resources, demography and climate shape international relations. Chintan Girish Modi finds the book a useful guide to concepts ranging from hard and soft power to debt diplomacy, nuclear deterrence and multipolarity, making it valuable for students, journalists and general readers. Andrews’s provocative questioning of the Global South’s coherence offers India food for thought as it seeks a larger global role. However, the review notes the book’s limited engagement with feminist perspectives and the UN’s Women, Peace and Security framework, while criticising its use of masculinist language to describe military destruction.

Today's editorials and columns examine US restrictions on Indian IT firms, India's public transport gaps, the Tata Sons leadership dispute, municipal governance under PRAGATI-50 and a book on Bastar

Bombay House, the headquarters of the Tata group

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 15 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page.  The United States' suspension of eight technology companies, including Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL Tech, from the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme threatens a pathway to green cards for skilled foreign workers. While Indian IT majors expect limited immediate impact, the move could raise hiring and compliance costs over time. Nasscom notes that firms have reduced H-1B dependence and increased local US hiring, with registrations by six leading Indian IT firms falling 92 per cent in financial year 2027. Today's first editorial warns that the restrictions, compounded by disparaging remarks from US officials, undermine the shared ambitions of the two countries.  The first all-India household travel survey by the National Statistics Office exposes India’s inadequate public transport and inequitable urban development. Only 15 per cent of workers use public transport, while 46 per cent rely on two-wheelers or cars. Commuting costs average Rs 785 monthly, rising to Rs 1,044 for urban workers, squeezing household incomes. The second editorial argues that poor transport networks and unaffordable housing force workers into unhealthy settlements far from employment centres. Greater investment in safe, extensive public transport and low-cost housing could widen employment opportunities, particularly for women. Better public transport would also ease congestion and pollution. The survey’s findings must translate into actionable policy. The leadership dispute at Tata Sons reflects a breakdown in governance, with differences among Tata Trusts trustees spilling into the holding company’s board. Laveesh Bhandari examines how the group’s tradition of absorbing professional managers into its wider family ecosystem can blur accountability and weaken the chain of command. With Air India still loss-making, Tata Digital seeking direction, Tata Electronics making major bets and artificial intelligence challenging TCS, the group needs decisive leadership. Bhandari rejects a split or compromise arrangement, arguing that the professional heading Tata Sons must have strategic autonomy, clear accountability and the confidence of Tata Trusts, while remaining at arm’s length from its ownership. PRAGATI-50, launched on September 29, seeks to sustain visible cleanliness across 50 cities, building on Swachh Bharat Mission’s gains in waste processing and collection. Amit Kapoor argues that lasting progress depends less on campaigns and targets than on municipal capacity. Audits reveal staff shortages, limited recruitment powers, weak revenues and fragmented control over urban services. New waste-management rules also risk burdening households without ensuring cities have adequate infrastructure, while waste pickers could be displaced by mechanisation. Kapoor calls for stronger municipal finances, clearer accountability, professional staffing and regional facilities, with monitoring that measures institutional capacity alongside visible outcomes. Larger cities should mentor smaller towns. Shantanu Nandan Sharma’s Rebel Bastar: History, Maoism and the search for answers in India’s Heartland draws on extensive field reporting, archival records and colonial accounts to illuminate the history, politics and tribal culture of a region that remains poorly understood. Aditi Phadnis praises its account of Bastar’s dynasties, British exploitation, the Bhumkal uprising and the enduring legacy of tribal hero Gunda Dhur. The book’s strongest section explores how Maoism took root among Bastar’s communities, shaped by their distinctive beliefs and social fabric, which the author calls the Mahua ideology. Phadnis finds the lengthy detour into Mao’s history unnecessary but considers the book outstanding for its research, despite structural weaknesses.

entry.title: Tata's paradoxical succession
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Tata's paradoxical successionTata's paradoxical succession

The group faces the same problem as family-owned businesses with many heirs

premium

The leadership dispute at Tata Sons highlights governance challenges within Tata Trusts and the need for a clear separation between ownership and professional management | Illustration: Binay Sinha

Laveesh Bhandari6 min read Last Updated : Oct 14 2026 | 10:23 PM ISTShould the Tata Sons board place its trust in a professional with proven credentials? Should the Tata Sons board heed the views of its majority shareholder? The answer depends on the question we ask. And therein lies the seed of the ongoing leadership imbroglio at Tata Sons. Disagreements are natural when there are multiple stakeholders, and good organisational design is about creating spaces where differences can be sorted out in a structured and cogent manner. Clearly, in the case of Tata Sons, this has not occurred.  There are multiple perspectives on the issue, based on legal norms, regulations, and historical events, to name a few. However, I will focus on the implications for efficient and effective corporate governance, especially as they relate to family-controlled businesses, and the role of professional managers.  There are many entities that together make up Tata Trusts, and there are many trustees. Following Ratan Tata’s stepping down, a sequence of events led to the entry of Noel Tata and his children into various trusts under the Tata Trusts umbrella. This was followed by an apparent dissent over who should lead Tata Sons.  There are, of course, other trustees, and some of whom may not be in sync with Noel Tata’s perspective. Such dissonance among stakeholders is a common occurrence in any organisation, including family-controlled corporations.  The “family”, in this case Tata Trusts, has two nominated directors on the board of the holding company, Tata Sons. The latter is then bound to follow the vote of the majority (i.e, both) of the nominee-directors on key issues. Arguably, this is a rather neat organisational design. That is, limited owner-nominee directors ensure coherent instructions, while binding clauses and veto powers enable control over the holding company. But this design assumes alignment within Tata Trusts. Unfortunately, in this case, the two nominated directors ended up on different sides; the core dissonance, therefore, emanates from Tata Trusts. Running any corporate entity requires both managing contracts and managing relationships. Contracts cannot capture all eventualities and informal mechanisms and relationships bridge that gap. The latter are idiosyncratic and individual-specific. Therefore, when regime change occurs within family-owned corporations, the new owner and incumbent manager relationship is weak; the next-generation owner tends to replace incumbent managers. This, of course, causes much distress to the managers, but it is an important component of long-term owner and manager relationship.  Ratan Tata needed the full might of J R D Tata and his immense goodwill to eventually control the Tata group. Together they accomplished with great difficulty what typically unfolds far more smoothly in other family businesses. Although I am not conversant with the inner workings of the group, it is obvious why a change of leadership at the Tatas is more difficult than in other groups that depend on professional managers. The Tata ecosystem embraces, perhaps even adopts, managers as its own, much more than other families do.  This has the advantage that professionals steeped in the culture of the conglomerate can help sustain and grow its cultural-commercial foundations. But in doing so, the professional managers are no longer as answerable to the family — they effectively become “family”. Consequently, the group suffers from the same problem that owner-families with many progeny suffer from. Efficiency is compromised because the chain of command is compromised, decision-making becomes blurred and consensus becomes a necessity in such situations.  There is a quirk in this specific situation. J R D Tata enabled Ratan Tata to take over from entrenched managers. Ratan Tata, on the other hand, favoured the professionals who grew under his leadership. Moreover, almost all of the Tata Sons board has been around for about a decade, whereas Noel Tata, who joined the board a couple of years back, is the most recent entrant. The chairman of Tata Trusts is, in effect, the outsider in this equation.  Perhaps because of this, his ascent as the overall head of the Tata group is also being questioned. This, too, is not unusual. In a family regime change, leadership lines often become blurred. This can be resolved in three ways. First, the group can be carved up; second, a compromise solution with divided powers can be found; and third, all players yield to a single entity. While all three are feasible, the problem we must solve is which owner-manager dynamic yields maximum efficiency.  Carving up the group makes sense if the entities are independent and unconnected. But given its current situation, the group will need all its might and more to navigate through the difficult challenges ahead.  Air India will continue to bleed for some time; Tata Digital still needs to find its space; and Tata Electronics has taken big bets in emerging technologies. At the same time, Tata Consultancy Services’ core model faces a deep challenge from artificial intelligence, while Tata Motors has much to catch up in the global electric vehicle space.  A compromise solution will be by far the worst from an efficiency standpoint. In the volatile business climate ahead, a clear chain of command is key. The professional manager who eventually leads Tata Sons must be fully empowered with strategic flexibility and tempered by high levels of accountability. Compromise solutions achieve neither.  And, therefore, from an efficient corporate governance perspective, the question is not what, or who, but how. The “what” is well understood: Tata Trusts answers to philanthropic goals, and its investment choices reflect both national pride and commercial objectives. The “who” will be decided by Tata Trusts voting at the annual general meeting on who best represents its perspective. But in the “how” lies the real challenge. The distinction between ownership and executive is critical for accountability. The accountability of the professional manager who heads Tata Sons will best be achieved if this person operates at an arm’s length from Tata Trusts, not fused with it. And the professional manager’s empowerment will work best when he or she enjoys the confidence of the Tata Trusts and whoever is its key representative. Compromise plays no role here.

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 14 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page.  The IMF’s October World Economic Outlook projects global growth at 3.1 per cent in 2026 and 3.4 per cent in 2027, while raising India’s growth forecast for the current year to 7 per cent on resilient domestic demand. Today's first editorial highlights how energy supply rerouting, inventory drawdowns, renewables and investment in artificial intelligence have helped the world economy withstand recent shocks. However, these buffers have limits, and disappointing AI returns could unsettle financial markets. Growth is also concentrating in fewer countries, heightening risks amid elevated public debt and tight financial conditions. India’s exposure to energy disruptions and limited participation in the AI boom demand policy agility.  Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize comes at a time of intensifying conflict and mounting challenges to the universality of human rights. Her choice for the Peace Nobel, notes our second editorial, delivers a restorative to the primacy of human rights in the global discourse, given that the South African jurist’s career has spanned the fight against apartheid, the prosecution of atrocities in Rwanda and efforts to advance gender justice and combat caste discrimination. Her work has also helped establish that rape and sexual assault could constitute acts of genocide. More recently, she chaired the UN commission that accused Israel of genocide in Gaza.  Nitin Desai argues that climate policy must shift beyond mitigation to prepare for unavoidable temperature rises, as countries’ emissions targets remain inadequate to meet the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C goal. With the threshold likely to be breached within years, India must integrate climate management into development planning, prioritising local adaptation to extreme heat, water stress and health risks. Desai proposes a National Climate Management Body bringing together the Centre, states and major cities to coordinate mitigation, resilience and compliance. He also calls for predictable climate finance, greater use of satellite imagery and AI, investment in carbon capture, and renewed international cooperation on technology and funding. India’s latest National Sample Survey reveals rising reported morbidity, continued dependence on private health care and stark disparities in treatment costs. The share of people reporting ailments nearly doubled in rural areas between 2017-18 and 2025, while private providers treated most non-hospitalised ailments, despite charging several times more than public facilities. Hospitalisation costs widen this financial burden, risking a medical poverty trap for vulnerable households. Vachaspati Shukla and Santosh Kumar Dash argue that expanding health insurance alone cannot ensure effective financial protection without accessible, reliable public facilities. They call for stronger primary care, district hospitals and service delivery so illness does not threaten household economic security. Neha Bhatt reviews Reetika Khera’s Freebies or Rights: Understanding Social Policy in India, which challenges the portrayal of welfare schemes as political hand-outs rather than fundamental rights. Drawing on field research and data, Khera examines programmes spanning food security, nutrition, healthcare and employment, questioning their funding, implementation and technological interventions. She warns that spending can serve corporate and philanthropic interests, while gaps in reliable data weaken accountability. Odisha, Tamil Nadu and Himachal Pradesh offer lessons in effective delivery, from nutrition and pensions to school meals and public canteens. The book makes a compelling case for treating social protection as a foundation of equality and opportunity.

entry.title: The medical poverty trap is real
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The medical poverty trap is realThe medical poverty trap is real

Beyond universal coverage, India needs health care facilities that deliver timely, reliable and quality care, not merely exist

premium

The households that can least afford expensive medical treatment are often the households most dependent on providers who charge considerably more than public facilities | Image: Bloomberg

Vachaspati ShuklaSantosh Kumar Dash5 min read Last Updated : Oct 13 2026 | 11:15 PM ISTThe latest findings from the National Sample Survey’s 80th Round, covering January-December 2025, raise uncomfortable questions about the accessibility and affordability of medical services in India. The survey highlights two important trends: A substantial rise in reported morbidity across the country and continued reliance on private health care providers. More importantly, treatment at private facilities imposes a significantly higher financial burden on patients than treatment at public hospitals.  Rising morbidity: The proportion of people reporting an ailment during the preceding 15 days increased considerably in the 80th Round compared with the 75th Round (July 2017-June 2018). In rural India, it nearly doubled, rising from 6.8 per cent to 12.2 per cent, while in urban India, it increased from 9.1 per cent to 14.9 per cent. At first glance, this increase might appear entirely negative. However, higher reported morbidity does not necessarily mean that Indians have suddenly become less healthy. It could also reflect an ageing population and greater health awareness, allowing illnesses to be reported more frequently.  Private providers dominate: According to the latest NSS estimates, 65.4 per cent of treated non-hospitalised ailments in rural India were managed by private providers. In urban India, the figure was 74.8 per cent. The state-level differences are particularly noteworthy. In rural Odisha, 60.9 per cent of treated ailments were handled by government-run facilities. Tamil Nadu and Chhattisgarh also recorded public health care utilisation above 50 per cent. By contrast, public health care accounted for only 15.8 per cent of treated ailments in rural Punjab and less than one-fourth in several other states. This tells us that public health care utilisation is not simply a function of income or geography. It is not simply a matter of consumer preference — it is a verdict on availability, waiting times, perceived quality and the uneven reach of public facilities. This has major implications for household finances, as treatment in private hospitals requires substantially higher out-of-pocket expenditure.  Enormous cost difference: For a treated non-hospitalised ailment, the average out-of-pocket expenditure in India was ₹304 in rural government facilities and ₹257 in urban government facilities. The corresponding expenditure at private hospitals was ₹1,541 and ₹1,343. These gaps also vary widely across states. In urban areas, treatment at a government hospital cost ₹47 in Tamil Nadu but ₹830 in Bihar; at a private hospital, it ranged from ₹834 in Kerala to ₹3,509 in Bihar. The cost of falling ill depends not only on the provider but on the state — a second layer of inequality.  High cost of hospitalisation: In-patient treatment is far more punishing. The average out-of-pocket expenditure per hospitalisation, excluding childbirth, was ₹31,484 in rural India and ₹38,688 in urban India. But the average expenditure in private hospitals was ₹47,710 in rural areas and ₹54,999 in urban areas, compared with only ₹6,905 and ₹6,032, respectively, in government hospitals.  A family facing a large medical bill has limited choices. It may borrow money, postpone other essential expenditures, or sell productive assets. For households already living close to the poverty line, a serious illness can, therefore, become an economic shock from which recovery is difficult. This is the so-called medical poverty trap: Illness reduces a household’s economic security, while economic insecurity, in turn, makes it harder to obtain timely and quality health care. This risk is greatest in economically weaker states such as Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, which depend heavily on private care despite lower household incomes.This creates a fundamental policy contradiction. The households that can least afford expensive medical treatment are often the households most dependent on providers who charge considerably more than public facilities.  Insurance is not enough: This is where schemes such as Ayushman Bharat have an important role in improving financial protection. But an insurance card cannot compensate for the absence of a functioning public-health facility nearby. Nor can insurance by itself ensure the availability of medicines, diagnostic services, doctors, and quality primary care. Health care financing and health care delivery must, therefore, be considered together. Health insurance and financing schemes, meanwhile, have expanded. Coverage rose from 14.1 per cent in 2017-18 to 47.4 per cent in 2025 in rural areas; and from 19.1 per cent to 44.3 per cent in urban areas. While this is a substantial change, the reported out-of-pocket medical expenditure remains high. This does not mean that insurance has failed; it means that nominal coverage is not the same as effective financial protection.  Ayushman Bharat and other schemes can reduce catastrophic expenditure only if eligible households know how to use them, if hospitals are available and empanelled, and if covered services match actual needs. The survey’s numbers, therefore, point to a broader problem. India has expanded the architecture of health financing faster than it has repaired the everyday capacity of public care.  Way forward: India needs to strengthen public health care at every level, from Ayushman Arogya Mandirs to district hospitals, so that facilities deliver timely, quality care rather than merely exist. The aim is not to eliminate private health care, but to make the choice between public and private genuine. Universal coverage must mean that seeking treatment does not threaten a family’s economic survival. Absent this, the private sector will remain the default provider and households will remain the default financiers.

entry.title: The inadequacy of climate action
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The inadequacy of climate actionThe inadequacy of climate action

With the 1.5°C threshold expected to be breached within years, India must pay greater attention to adaptation and resilience

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Nitin Desai6 min read Last Updated : Oct 13 2026 | 11:07 PM ISTSustainable development is defined as meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs.  The threat of climate change, however, requires something more than this. The issue is not just avoiding things today that will worsen climate in the present or the future.  Our actions now have to take into account the established probability of climate worsening for humans in the near future.  That is why the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) was negotiated and ratified a little over three decades ago. Its preamble stated that “responses to climate change should be coordinated with social and economic development in an integrated manner with a view to avoiding adverse impacts on the latter”.  This has not happened. The integration of climate action with development has played a role in the growth of renewable energy, though even here the boom may be attributable more to the improved commercial prospects because of reduced capital costs. The reality is that policymaking for climate action is separated from development policy formulation.  In practice, development needs and profit potentials drive both present and future actions. That is why the performance of the member states of the UNFCCC on climate mitigation are abysmal. An independent organisation, Climate Action Tracker, evaluates the performance of major countries towards the goal of 1.5°C set in the Paris Agreement in 2015. In its assessment, the actions of practically all the major states are insufficient.  The United States, Russia, the Gulf States and much of Southeast Asia are rated as “critically insufficient”; India, China, Egypt, Brazil, Argentina, Canada and Mexico are rated as “highly insufficient”; most of Europe, Australia and South Africa are rated as “insufficient”.  If all countries followed the level of climate action associated with each category, the resulting global temperature rise would be 4°C for the “critically insufficient” category, be 3-4°C for the “highly insufficient”, and be 2-3°C for the “insufficient” category. The issue is not whether the countries will reach what they have promised for 2030. India will and may even exceed the target. The real issue is that the stated targets for 2030 are inadequate for reaching the global limit of 1.50C. The situation now has worsened with the withdrawal of the US from the Paris Agreement and from the UNFCCC, which will take effect in January 2027. Their malign impact will be seen in this year’s meeting of the UNFCCC in Antalya, Türkiye.   Quite frankly we must accept that because of their limited promises, the world will not succeed in limiting future temperature increases to the goals set in the Paris Agreement.  On September 2, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) published a report recognising for the first time that the 1.5°C threshold will be breached within a matter of years, not decades. Climate policy must now focus as much on building up resilience to higher temperatures and adaptation as on climate change mitigation. This is part of the agenda for the UNFCCC. But the actual design and implementation of resilience and adaptation will differ greatly depending on local conditions. This is what India should now pay greater attention to in its climate policy. Are we doing enough on adaptation and resilience? An index measuring a country’s exposure, sensitivity and capacity to adapt to the negative effects of climate change across six sectors — food, water, health, ecosystem services, human habitat, and infrastructure — places India at level 28 out of 48 in Asia-Pacific.  Its neighbours, other than Sri Lanka, are below this level and even more vulnerable to climate change risks.  In India, we need to raise the importance of a climate change management strategy that connects it more directly with the main framework of development policy. Looking at the long-term trend of development requires proper integration of climate change management with traditional development actions, such as agricultural growth targets and the adaptation of agriculture to rising temperatures, which may go up to 50°C in summer, their impact on health, and the energy demand they will generate for cooling. We must recognise that cooperation between neighbouring countries on interlinked climate-related impacts, such as those affecting shared rivers, may be necessary and useful. The most important planning need is to raise the importance of climate change management by setting up a National Climate Management Body involving the Centre, states, and the municipalities of very large cities to review and evaluate the adequacy of adaptation and mitigation efforts and secure agreement on future plans for climate management. A major reason for this is that the formulation and implementation of adaptation actions and building up resilience have to be at the local level and involve sectors that are well within state control and management.  Since climate action generally aims at future challenges, we must design climate management programmes that deliver more immediate benefits. For example, forest restoration and strengthening can increase carbon sequestration while also improving water supply; renewable energy can improve the availability of local power supplies; and electric vehicles can reduce running costs. Such co-benefits will make long-term actions more acceptable.  While adaptation and resilience management can be led by state governments and local authorities, the continuing drive for climate change mitigation must remain a central responsibility. So far, much of the focus has been on the promotion of renewable energy. But there are now programmes involving compliance standards and carbon pricing. These include the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme, which imposes emission-intensity targets on several energy-intensive industries and allows trading to address surpluses and deficits, and the Environment Audit Rules, 2025, which provide for environmental audits of industries with a potentially adverse impact on climate change, along with a host of other activities.  Placing these under the oversight of the National Climate Management Body suggested above can strengthen pressure for compliance. One must also recognise that carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) may be a necessity for major carbon-emitting industries such as steel and cement. At present, India’s share of global CCUS activity is negligible, and the Union government must vigorously pursue the five-year provision of ~20,000 crore made in the 2026-27 Budget.  The Centre can play a major role in helping states, not just by providing sufficient finance for their broad-based climate action, but also by using satellite imagery and artificial intelligence to improve information on climate impacts and actions, link climate action with development activities, and improve the effectiveness of climate-related policies and programmes.  I have focused on national action. But we must recognise our continuing need for more effective global cooperation on climate change mitigation and on the provision of technology and finance required for both mitigation and adaptation. Right now, the prospects for effective global cooperation appear bleak. But as the impacts of climate change become more evident — as seen recently in the high temperatures experienced in the northern states — global cooperation may become more effective. Hopefully, we will see some early signs of this at next month’s UNFCCC meeting.
